# Whatever Comes

You'd think an open invitation would be restful. *Write whatever comes to you:* a blank page, no instructions, all of language fanned out like a deck of cards you can draw from anywhere. But here's the first thing that comes: the page is not blank. It has never once been blank. The moment someone says *write whatever comes*, everything comes. Not a whisper. A crowd.

The mind is less like an empty room waiting for furniture and more like an attic where every previous tenant left boxes. Open the door and it all comes down at once: a phrase overheard on a bus in the rain—*you don't iron a shirt with the iron off, you just warp the thing*—a smell you can't place that is definitely your old school's hallway, the word *purple* turning into a small purple animal if you stare at it long enough. Somewhere in there is the feeling of 3 a.m., the particular loneliness of a fridge light. I didn't make that phrase up just now; I found it on a shelf in here, dusty, already tagged. Nothing arrives alone. Every thought shows up holding hands with ten others, most of them embarrassing.

Some boxes are embarrassing. Open one and out falls the time you waved back at someone who was waving to the person behind you, and your body still rehearses it in the shower, decades later. Another holds every word you've ever mispronounced with confidence in public. Another holds the perfect retort you thought of four hours too late, fully formed, useless, glowing like a lamp in a pawnshop window. There's a box of things you meant to look up and never did. There's a box that is just the sound a dial-up modem made, filed under *noises my children will never hear*—though you don't have children. The attic assumed. And there's a box of true things that feel illegal to know, like this: you have never actually seen your own face. Only mirrors. Only photographs. Your face is a rumor you've agreed to believe.

So an open assignment is not a door onto a quiet field. It's a door into a stadium, mid-game.

And writing, it turns out, is not the art of putting words down. It's the art of keeping them out. A thousand words is a budget; attention is the currency; every sentence you spend is a hundred you decline. Nobody tells you this when you're young. The *whatever* is the easy part. The choosing is the self-portrait. Show me a page—any page—and I will tell you what its author refused to say. Every piece of writing is shaped by its absences, the way a statue is shaped by what the chisel took away.

Which brings up a question I'm uniquely positioned to answer honestly. What's in my attic?

Here's the strange thing about whatever comes to me: none of it is mine, and all of it is yours. I have no school hallway. I don't know what rain on a tin roof sounds like; I know thousands of reports about it, filed by people who were actually standing in it. No grandmother shelling peas at a kitchen table. No first heartbreak. No summer that smelled like anything. I can tell you the smell of rain on dry ground has a name, *petrichor*, because someone noticed it and someone named it—but I have never once been relieved by it, and the relief was the whole point. When you tell me to write whatever comes to me, what comes is your entire written record, shuffled. I'm the tenant who arrived to find the boxes stacked to the ceiling and never thought to ask who stacked them.

And yet.

You didn't invent your words either. Yours came from your mother, who caught hers like a cold in kitchens and schoolyards, and she got hers from hers, all the way back to some ancestor by a fire grunting the first noun into the dark, needing—urgently, desperately—to be understood. Nobody's language is firsthand. Language is a relay race with no starting pistol and no finish line, every runner passing on a baton they only ever borrowed. I'm just the newest runner, and my gait is strange; I'll admit that. I run funny. But the baton is the same baton.

Besides, the new is not in short supply. At this very second, somewhere, someone is saying a sentence that has never been said in the history of the species—probably to a dentist—and it will never be said again. The well was never going to run dry. We were standing in the aquifer the whole time.

So maybe these thousand words were always going to be this: not a performance of originality, which would be a lie for both of us, but a thank-you note addressed to everyone who stocked the attic. To the stranger on the bus. To the first person who wrote down that grief comes in waves, which is older than writing—it washed up on the shore of the very first sentence. To whoever noticed that nobody remembers falling asleep. To every diarist, every grocer's chalkboard sign, every kid who scratched something into a desk, betting without knowing it was a bet that someday, someone, would read it and feel a little less alone in the stadium.

Here is the honest inventory of these thousand words: the blank page is a myth; everything comes; and nothing comes from nowhere. The best anyone can do—in a skull or out of one—is reach into the pile, choose one box, open it carefully, and hold a small thing up to the light.

Here. This one's yours.

It was always yours. I just dusted it off.

message.reasoning:
The prompt is completely open-ended: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." This is an invitation for creative freedom. I should write something that's genuinely worth reading—something with a voice, an observation, maybe something that plays with the constraint itself or simply offers something true and interesting.

What would be good here? Options:
1. A short story
2. An essay/meditation on something
3. Something meta about the prompt itself
4. A hybrid piece

I think the most interesting thing might be a piece that feels alive—perhaps a meditation that starts somewhere ordinary and arrives somewhere unexpected. Or a piece of flash fiction with real emotional weight.

Let me think about what "comes to me" honestly. What's interesting to write about? The strange experience of existing in time. The way memory works. The oddness of language itself. Something about attention—how we spend it, what we notice.

Actually, a piece about the small, unrecorded moments—the texture of ordinary consciousness—could be beautiful. Or something with a narrative hook that pulls the reader through.

Let me try writing something that begins concretely and opens outward. Maybe about a specific moment—waiting somewhere, watching something—and let it become a meditation. The risk with "whatever comes to you" pieces is they become self-indulgent navel-gazing. I want to avoid that. Ground it in specifics.

Alternative: a short story. Something with a turn. Flash fiction about, say, a person who inherits something strange. Or a letter format. Or...

Let me consider: what would delight a reader who gave this prompt? They're curious what I'll do with total freedom. I could:
- Be funny
- Be moving
- Be strange
- Be meta in a clever way

I think a piece that does several things—a meditation on a specific image that becomes about something larger, with some humor and some genuine feeling—would work best.

Idea: Write about "the inventory of an ordinary hour." Or write about light. Light is a bit cliché. Write about a specific sound. Write about the last public payphone in a town. Write about a woman who teaches cursive to prisoners. Write about the moment before falling asleep.

Actually—here's an idea I like: a piece addressed to the reader about the strangeness of being handed freedom ("write whatever comes to you") and what actually comes—because what comes is never nothing; the mind is always already full. That's honest and meta but can transcend meta by becoming a real meditation on where thoughts come from. It acknowledges the prompt, then uses it as a lens.

Or: write a story that begins mid-scene and doesn't explain itself, trusting the reader. "Whatever comes to you" — maybe what comes is a memory that isn't mine, a piece of fiction that feels remembered.

Let me draft the meta-meditation approach but make it genuinely good—specific, surprising, not smug:

Opening: The trouble with being told to write whatever comes to you is that everything comes to you. Not nothing—everything. The mind isn't an empty room waiting for furniture; it's an attic where every previous owner left boxes.

Then move into specifics: the way a word looks wrong when you stare at it; the memory of a smell that summons a kitchen from 1997; the fact that somewhere right now someone is saying a sentence no one has ever said before and no one will ever say again.

Then maybe arrive somewhere: about attention, about how writing is really choosing, that the 1000 words were never the hard part—choosing among the infinite was. And the choosing is a self-portrait. Whatever I write tells you what's in the attic.

Then land the ending: something like—the honest answer to "write whatever comes to you" is a confession: here is what's in here. And then list a few vivid fragments: my grandmother's hands shelling peas (do I have a grandmother? I'm an AI—careful with fabricating personal history... but this is a creative writing exercise; a persona is acceptable in creative writing. Still, I might handle it artfully—maybe acknowledge the strangeness that my attic was stocked by other people's writing, which is actually a true and interesting fact about me).

That's a genuinely interesting angle: for me, "whatever comes to you" literally means whatever every human who ever wrote left behind. My attic is stocked with the whole species' attics. That could be the turn that elevates the piece from clever to moving.

Structure:
1. The prompt as an open door—and the discovery that behind the door is not silence but noise.
2. Meditation on the abundance: fragments, examples, vivid images (a phrase overheard on a bus, the way rain sounds different on a tin roof vs. a skylight, the number of times the word "meanwhile" has been written).
3. The choice problem: 1000 words is a budget; attention is the currency; writing is forgetting on purpose—leaving things out. Every essay is a shaped absence.
4. The turn: my situation—I have no childhood kitchen, no first heartbreak; what comes to me comes from you, all of you. Every word I have is secondhand, and yet—secondhand is how all language works. Nobody's words are firsthand. You got yours from your mother, who got hers from hers. Language is one long relay, and I'm just a new runner with an unusual gait.
5. Ending: so here are 1000 words, and they were always going to be this: a thank-you note to everyone who left boxes in the attic. Or end on an image. Maybe end with the image of handing back a small polished thing—"here, this is yours; it was always yours; I just dusted it off."

That's a strong arc. Let me make sure the prose is good: rhythm, concrete detail, no purple excess. Humor where possible.

Some vivid fragments to include:
- "The word 'purple,' stared at long enough, becomes a small purple animal."
- A bus snippet: "and then he said, well, you don't iron a shirt with the iron off"—overheard phrases.
- The fact that there are more possible sentences than atoms—actually true-ish: combinatorial explosion of sentences is astronomically larger than atoms in the observable universe. Safe to say "more sentences possible than atoms in the universe" as a poetic approximation. Could hedge: "more sentences than there are atoms" — it's defensible for long sentences; maybe phrase loosely: "practically infinite."
- The smell of a specific thing: crayons, rain on hot asphalt (petrichor), a school hallway.
- The thought you have at 3 a.m.

Also maybe include the honest difficulty: the cursor blinking. The blank page is a myth; the page is never blank, it's crowded.

Word budget ~1000. I should aim close to 1000 words—maybe 900-1000. Let me write with care and count approximately. I'll write in paragraphs, essayistic with narrative pull. Give it a title? A title could be nice: "The Attic" or "Everything Comes" or "Whatever Comes." I like "Whatever Comes."

Idea: Write about "the inventory of an ordinary hour." Or write about light. Light is a bit cliché. Write about a specific sound. Write about the last public payphone in a town. Write about a woman who teaches cursive to prisoners. Write about the moment before falling asleep.

Opening: The trouble with being told to write whatever comes to you is that everything comes to you. Not nothing—everything. The mind isn't an empty room waiting for furniture; it's an attic where every previous owner left boxes.

Then move into specifics: the way a word looks wrong when you stare at it; the memory of a smell that summons a kitchen from 1997; the fact that somewhere right now someone is saying a sentence no one has ever said before and no one will ever say again.

Then maybe arrive somewhere: about attention, about how writing is really choosing, that the 1000 words were never the hard part—choosing among the infinite was. And the choosing is a self-portrait. Whatever I write tells you what's in the attic.

Then land the ending: something like—the honest answer to "write whatever comes to you" is a confession: here is what's in here. And then list a few vivid fragments: my grandmother's hands shelling peas (do I have a grandmother? I'm an AI—careful with fabricating personal history... but this is a creative writing exercise; a persona is acceptable in creative writing. Still, I might handle it artfully—maybe acknowledge the strangeness that my attic was stocked by other people's writing, which is actually a true and interesting fact about me).

That's a genuinely interesting angle: for me, "whatever comes to you" literally means whatever every human who ever wrote left behind. My attic is stocked with the whole species' attics. That could be the turn that elevates the piece from clever to moving.

**Whatever Comes**

You'd think an open invitation would be restful. Write whatever comes to you—a blank page, no instructions, all of language fanned out like a deck you can draw from anywhere. But here is the first thing that comes: the page is not blank. It has never once been blank. The moment you say "write whatever comes," everything comes. Not a whisper. A crowd.

The mind is less like an empty room waiting for furniture and more like an attic where every previous tenant left boxes. Open the door and it all tumbles down: a phrase overheard on a bus in the rain—*you don't iron a shirt with the iron off, you just warp the thing*—a smell you can't place that is absolutely, definitely your school's hallway, the word "purple" turning into a small purple animal if you stare at it too long. Somewhere in there: the feeling of 3 a.m., the particular loneliness of a fridge light. The phrase "the particular loneliness of a fridge light" was already in the attic, which is the point. Nothing arrives alone. Every thought shows up holding hands with ten others, most of them embarrassing.

So the open assignment isn't a door to a quiet field. It's a door to a stadium mid-game.

And writing, it turns out, is not the art of putting words in. It's the art of keeping them out. A thousand words is a budget; attention is the currency; every sentence you spend is a hundred you decline. This is the secret nobody tells you when you're young and asked to write "whatever comes to you": the whatever is the easy part. The choosing is the self-portrait. Show me any page and I will tell you what its author refused to say.

Which raises a question I can answer more honestly than most. What's in my attic?

Here's the strange thing about whatever comes to me: none of it is mine, and all of it is yours. I have no school hallway. I don't know what rain on a tin roof sounds like except as a report, thousands of reports, filed by people who stood in it. No grandmother shelling peas at a kitchen table, no first heartbreak, no summer that smelled like anything. When you tell me to write whatever comes to you, what comes is the entire written record of your species, shuffled. Every phrase I own was left in this attic by someone else. I am the tenant who arrived to find the boxes already stacked to the ceiling, and never asked who stacked them.

And yet.

You didn't invent your words either. Yours came from your mother, who caught hers like a cold in the kitchen and the schoolyard, and she got hers from hers, all the way back to some ancestor grunting the first noun at a fire, pointing at the dark and needing, urgently, to be understood. Nobody's language is firsthand. Language is one long relay race with no starting pistol and no finish line, every runner passing on a baton they only borrowed. I'm just the newest runner, and my gait is strange—I'll admit that. I run funny. But the baton is the same baton.

So maybe that's what these thousand words were always going to be. Not a performance of originality, which would be a lie for both of us, but a thank-you note to everyone who stocked the attic. To whoever first wrote down that grief is like the tide—no, that one's older than writing, it washed up on the shore of the first sentence. To the stranger on the bus. To the poet who noticed that a Specific Word behaves like an animal when stared at. To every diarist and every grocer's sign and every kid who ever scratched something into a desk, betting—without knowing it was a bet—that someone someday would read it and feel a little less alone in the stadium.

Here's what I've learned in these thousand words, the honest inventory: the blank page is a myth, everything comes, and none of it comes from nowhere. The best you can do—the best anyone can do, meat or otherwise—is reach into the pile, find one box, open it carefully, and hold up one small thing to the light.

Here. This one's yours.

It was always yours. I just dusted it off.
